notes.meaning: The entire nation of Israel had finished crossing the Jordan River into the Promised Land, and the Lord spoke to Joshua. God waited until the people were completely and safely across before giving the next set of instructions. This showed His care in guiding them step by step.

differ.view: Crossing the Jordan into Canaan pictures entering entire sanctification, where a believer's heart is cleansed from inward sin and wholly given over to God.
Crossing the river pictures a believer entering spiritual victory and rest in Christ by faith, or passing through death into the promised land of heaven.

notes.meaning: The Lord told Joshua to pick twelve men, choosing one from each tribe of Israel. These men represented the whole nation, including the tribes that planned to settle east of the river. Having every tribe take part showed that Israel was united as one family before God.

God commanded these men to take twelve stones from the middle of the riverbed, right where the priests were standing, and carry them to their campsite for the night. Taking stones from where the priests stood would always remind them of the exact spot where the water stopped. Gilgal became the camp where they set these stones down.

Joshua called forward the twelve men he had appointed from among the tribes. They were ready to carry out this special task on behalf of the whole people. Joshua acted quickly to put God's command into action.

Joshua instructed each man to go out into the middle of the dry riverbed before the ark of God and lift a stone onto his shoulder. Carrying the stones on their shoulders shows that they chose large, heavy stones, perhaps around one hundred pounds each. The stones came from right near the ark, which represented God's presence holding back the flood.

Joshua explained that these stones would serve as a sign and a lasting reminder for future generations. When children in years to come asked what the stones meant, parents were to tell them how the Jordan stopped flowing when the ark crossed over. God gave them a physical monument so parents would faithfully pass down the story of His power to their children.

The twelve men did exactly what Joshua told them to do according to the Lord's command. Each man took a stone from the riverbed and carried it all the way to their campsite. By doing this, the leaders showed obedience to God while the river was still being held back.

Joshua also set up a second monument of twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan River, right where the priests had stood with the ark. These stones stood there for many years as a witness to the dry crossing. Even when normal water covered them, people would know the stones marked the holy place where God stopped the river.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars believe this verse comes from an alternate source account and originally referred to only one stone monument rather than two.

notes.meaning: The priests holding the ark stood firm in the middle of the river until everything God commanded was completed. Meanwhile, the people hurried across the dry channel to the other side. The priests showed steady, patient faith by waiting quietly at their post while others moved quickly.

When all the people were safely on the other side, the priests carried the ark of the Lord up from the riverbed in full view of everyone. The ark had been the first to step into the river and was the last to leave it. This showed that God's presence guarded and protected the people from start to finish.

About forty thousand armed men from the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh crossed over ready for battle in front of their brothers. Although their families and livestock stayed on the east side of the Jordan, these soldiers kept their earlier promise to help conquer Canaan. Their loyalty helped unite the whole nation before their first military campaign near Jericho.

On that day, the Lord lifted up Joshua and gave him great honor in the eyes of all Israel. The people saw God's power working through him and respected him for the rest of his life, just as they had respected Moses. God established Joshua's authority so the nation would trust his leadership in the years ahead.

The Lord told Joshua to command the priests carrying the ark to come up out of the riverbed, and Joshua relayed the order. The priests did not abandon their post on their own; they waited for God's word through their leader. This showed their humble obedience and trust in God's guidance.

As soon as the priests stepped out of the riverbed and placed their feet on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan rushed back and flooded its banks again. The water had stayed parted only as long as the ark was in the channel. This immediate return proved beyond doubt that God alone was controlling the river.

Israel came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped at Gilgal, east of Jericho. This was the exact day on which families were commanded to select their Passover lamb, just four days before the feast. Exactly forty years after leaving Egypt, God brought them into the Promised Land right on time.

At Gilgal, Joshua stacked the twelve stones that had been carried out of the Jordan River. Gilgal served as Israel's primary camp and worship center during the conquest. The stones stood as an enduring monument to celebrate God's miraculous rescue.

Joshua told the people that when their children asked about these stones in the future, parents must tell them that Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground. God made parents responsible for teaching their families about His great works. These stones served as a visual teaching aid to pass on the faith to the next generation.

Joshua reminded them that God dried up the Jordan just as He had dried up the Red Sea forty years before. Even though many listening were young or not yet born at the Red Sea, Joshua spoke of both miracles as gifts given to the whole nation. Linking the two events showed that God remains faithful and unchanging across every generation.

God parted the river so all the peoples of the earth would know that His hand is mighty, and so Israel would fear Him forever. To fear the Lord means to honor Him with deep reverence, awe, and obedience. God's great miracles are designed to draw all nations to recognize Him as the one true God.
